cms.summary: Who is the Divine Mother Kali, and what is our relationship with Her? In the days before Diwali and Kali Puja we look at Her as Brahman in manifestation, the power that has become this universe and all beings. We read the image at Dakshineswar detail by detail: Her dark complexion, Her feet on Siva, the garland of heads, the girdle of hands and the sword. We follow Sri Ramakrishna's own relationship with Her, Holy Mother as the motherhood of God in a human life, and Swami Vivekananda's long refusal and final acceptance. The class ends with Her four Shaktis in us, practices for the days of Diwali, and a prayer that all our powers be turned towards Her.
reflection_questions: What in my life looks dark or frightening mainly because I am standing far away from it?
Which person or thing in my day am I least able to see as Hers?
In which part of my life am I clinging like the monkey, and where could I mew like the kitten?
If I truly felt held, what fear would I put down today?
Which of my four powers is least aligned with my goal: my sense of “I”, my mind, my senses, or my dealings with things?

on: Diwali is near. On the new moon night of Kartik, Sunday 8 November 2026, the Divine Mother is worshipped as Kali. This class asks who She is and what our relationship with Her is, in the words of three people who knew Her: Sri Ramakrishna (1836 to 1886), Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi (1853 to 1920) and Swami Vivekananda (1863 to 1902).

The image on the screen is Bhavatarini, the Divine Mother at the Kali temple in Dakshineswar, where Sri Ramakrishna served as priest from 1855. Later in the evening we will read this image detail by detail: Her dark colour, Her feet on Siva, the garland of heads, the sword and the tongue.
gl: the Divine Mother as the power of time and of all change; from kāla, time
power or energy; the Divine as active
She who takes one across the ocean of worldly existence; the name of the image at Dakshineswar

paras: Diwali is near, and on the new moon night of Kartik the Divine Mother is worshipped as Kali. This class asks two questions. Who is this Divine Mother Kali? And what is our relationship with Her? The answers come from people who knew Her: Sri Ramakrishna, who worshipped Her at Dakshineswar and spoke with Her daily; Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi, whom he worshipped as the Divine Mother Herself; and Swami Vivekananda, who fought the idea of Kali for six years and then accepted Her as the power behind the universe.

The thread is a single question: whose lap am I sitting in? Vedanta answers that the power which has become this universe is not a stranger to us. She is the Mother, and we are Her children. Everything else tonight, the philosophy, the image, the practices, hangs on that one relationship.

The photograph is of Bhavatarini, the Divine Mother at the Kali temple in Dakshineswar on the Ganga, where Sri Ramakrishna was the priest from 1855. The same image he dressed, fed, sang to and argued with is the one we are looking at. Later in the evening we will read the image detail by detail.

deeper.h: IS THIS CLASS ONLY FOR HINDUS, OR ONLY FOR BENGALIS?
paras: No. The forms of worship described here grew in Bengal, and Swami Vivekananda was careful to say that Kali worship is not a necessary step in any religion. But the teaching behind the form is universal: that the power which has become this universe is not indifferent to us, that it can be approached as a mother, and that everything in our lives, pleasant and unpleasant, belongs to one Reality. Nobody is asked to adopt a practice. Everyone is invited to consider the teaching.

Sri Ramakrishna gives direct experience: he worshipped Her, spoke with Her, and reported what he saw. Holy Mother gives the motherhood of God in a human life, lived in a village kitchen and a Calcutta house. Swami Vivekananda gives the philosophy and the honest struggle: he rejected Kali for six years before accepting Her, and he could explain to a Western audience exactly what the image means.

on: The evening follows the old order of Vedantic learning: listening to the teaching, reflecting on it, and sitting quietly until it settles. Tonight reflection happens twice: in the questions marked on the slides during the talk, and in the question time at 7.15 pm.

New tonight: several slides carry a question in a green box. Some are for a minute of silence, some for the person beside you, some for the whole room. Four of them are marked with a star; if time is short we will use those. These slides are shared afterwards, so please do not photograph them.
gl: reflecting on it until doubts clear
sustained contemplation until it becomes one's own experience

paras: Arrival and refreshments from 6.15 pm, a guided meditation at 6.30, the talk from 6.45, questions and discussion at 7.15, and we close by 8.00. Please bring your questions. Tonight there is also discussion during the talk: several slides carry a question for you to sit with or to talk over with the person next to you.
